entry.title: How to Patch a Small Hole in Drywall
entry.summary: A hole up to about the size of a fist does not need a new piece of plasterboard. A self-adhesive mesh patch and two thin coats of compound will disappear …
entry.content:
A hole up to about the size of a fist does not need a new piece of plasterboard. A self-adhesive mesh patch and two thin coats of compound will disappear completely under paint — and unlike the old "stick a sponge in the hole" trick, it will not crack along the edge a year later.

Step 1: Cut the hole back to clean edges

Trim away any torn paper and loose crumbs with a utility knife so you are left with a clean square or circle. Feather the paper edge very slightly; a ragged paper lip is what makes a patch bulge.

Step 2: Apply the mesh patch

Peel the backing and centre the self-adhesive mesh over the hole, pressing it firmly onto sound plasterboard on all sides. The mesh is the reinforcement — without it, compound bridging a gap will crack.

Step 3: Two thin coats, not one thick one

Spread joint compound with a 100 mm knife, working from the edges inward, and leave it very slightly proud of the wall. Let it dry fully, then apply a second, wider coat that feathers out to nothing at the edges. One thick coat shrinks and cracks as it dries; two thin ones do not.

Step 4: Sand and prime

Sand with 120-grit paper wrapped round a flat block — never with your fingertips, which dig hollows. Prime the patch before painting, or the paint will flash: the patched area absorbs differently to the surrounding wall and shows as a dull spot.

What not to do

Do not skip the primer. It is the single most common reason a patch you cannot feel is still perfectly visible once the paint dries.

entry.title: How to Stop a Running Toilet
entry.summary: A cistern that keeps refilling is almost always the flapper — the rubber seal at the bottom of the tank that lifts when you flush. It costs very little, it can …
entry.content:
A cistern that keeps refilling is almost always the flapper — the rubber seal at the bottom of the tank that lifts when you flush. It costs very little, it can be swapped without turning off the house water, and it fixes the majority of running toilets in one go.

Step 1: Confirm it is the flapper

Take the lid off the cistern and put a few drops of food colouring in the tank. Do not flush. Wait fifteen minutes — if colour appears in the bowl, water is seeping past the flapper and that is your leak.

Step 2: Replace the flapper

Turn off the stop valve at the wall and flush to drain the tank. Unhook the old flapper from the two lugs at the base of the overflow tube and lift the chain off the flush lever. Fit the new one in the reverse order. If the chain has more than about 25 mm of slack it can catch under the new flapper, so shorten it.

Step 3: Check the fill level

If a new flapper does not fix it, look for water running down the overflow tube. That means the fill valve is set too high and is continuously topping up into the overflow. Most fill valves have an adjustment screw or a clip on the float — lower the waterline to roughly 25 mm below the top of the overflow tube.

What not to do

Do not reach for the cistern lid adjustment or start bending the float arm before doing the dye test. It takes fifteen minutes and tells you which of the two parts is actually at fault, instead of guessing at both.

entry.title: How to Unclog a Slow Draining Sink
entry.summary: A sink that drains slowly is telling you the blockage is partial and close to the surface. Skip the bottle of chemical drain cleaner — it rarely reaches the clog, it …
entry.content:
A sink that drains slowly is telling you the blockage is partial and close to the surface. Skip the bottle of chemical drain cleaner — it rarely reaches the clog, it sits in the trap eating at the pipe, and if it fails you have a basin of caustic water to work around. Start with the trap instead; it takes ten minutes and it is where most sink clogs actually are.

Step 1: Clear the trap

Put a bucket under the U-shaped pipe beneath the sink and unscrew the slip nuts by hand — they are designed to be hand-tight. Have the bucket ready before the last one comes off, because the trap is full of water by design. Tip the contents out and poke a bent wire hanger through the trap itself; hair and soap scum usually come out as a solid plug.

Step 2: Snake the wall arm

If the trap was clear, the blockage is further along, in the pipe running into the wall. A small hand auger — the cheap drum type with a cable — reaches the first metre or so, which is where the clog almost always sits. Feed the cable in gently and rotate; do not force it, because forced cable can scratch older metal pipe.

Step 3: Reassemble and test

Screw the trap back together by hand, then tighten a quarter turn with a wrench. Run the hot tap for a full minute and check the joint with a dry finger — any moisture at all means the slip nut needs another nudge.

What not to do

Do not use chemical drain cleaner repeatedly, and never use one immediately before opening the trap: caustic residue in the pipe ends up on your hands and in the bucket.

entry.title: How to Fix a Door That Won't Close
entry.summary: A door that suddenly refuses to latch is almost never a problem with the door itself. Nine times out of ten it is one of three things: loose hinge screws …
entry.content:
A door that suddenly refuses to latch is almost never a problem with the door itself. Nine times out of ten it is one of three things: loose hinge screws, a swollen frame, or a latch that has drifted out of line with the strike plate. Work through them in that order — it is the cheapest-first sequence, and the first fix resolves most cases.

Step 1: Tighten the hinge screws

Open the door and try lifting it by the handle. If it moves, the hinge screws have worked loose and the door is sagging onto the frame. Tighten every hinge screw, top to bottom. If a screw spins without biting, the hole is stripped — pull it out, glue in a wooden matchstick or a golf tee, snap it flush, and drive the screw back in.

Step 2: Check the strike plate

Close the door slowly and watch where the latch meets the strike plate. If it is catching on the top edge, the plate needs to move down; if on the bottom edge, up. Loosen the plate screws, tap it in the required direction with a hammer and a block of wood, then re-tighten. Filing the plate opening is a last resort — moving the plate is reversible, filing is not.

Step 3: Deal with a swollen frame

If the door binds along the whole latch side and the problem appeared in humid weather, the frame has swollen rather than the door dropping. Do not plane the door immediately. Run a dehumidifier in the room for a couple of days first, since the frame often shrinks back on its own. If it still binds, mark the high spots with a pencil held flat against the frame and plane only those.

What not to do

Resist the urge to plane the door first. It is irreversible, it is the messiest option, and in most cases the door was never too big — it was hanging slightly wrong.
